Figure 6. Comparison of flammability limits of LNG, LE, and jet fuel 1.1.5 Alternative Liquid Hydrocarbon Chemistries (Jet X) Jet X refers to non-drop-in liquid hydrocarbon synthetic aviation fuels. These fuels are under investigation and there is no agreed upon definition or composition of these fuels. The motivation to consider non-drop-in fuels is to identify potential properties that would increase efficiency and improve local airport air quality. These fuels are in the initial phases of investigation. ASTM has a non-drop-in jet fuel group to explore alternative chemistries. Currently, there is no ASTM standard for non-drop-in synthetic aviation fuels. There are substantial barriers to liquid aviation fuels that are not compatible with existing aircraft and fuel infrastructure. Extensive, long-term research on materials, aircraft, and infrastructure equipment would be needed to demonstrate compatibility and enable market acceptance. Another critical safety aspect is segregating Jet A/SAF at an airport from an alternate liquid aviation fuel to avoid contamination. Other barriers include potential resistance to microbial contamination, electrical capacitance differences, and impacts on fuel level readings (Dasgupta et al. 2023). 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Sustainable/Synthetic Aviation Fuel 2.1 Technical State of the Industry SAF currently must be blended with Jet A at a volume of up to 50 % to create compliant jet fuel. Once blended with Jet A, it exhibits the same technical capabilities of Jet A. SAF and Jet A share the same minimum net heat of combustion (lower heating value) of 42.8 MJ/kg per ASTM D1655, Standard Specification for Aviation Turbine Fuels (ASTM International 2025a), and ASTM D7566, Standard Specification for Aviation Turbine Fuel Containing Synthesized Hydrocarbons (ASTM International 2025b).2 Per ASTM D7566, SAF density at 15°C falls between 730 and 840 kg/m3 depending on technology pathway, whereas Jet A density falls between 775 and 840 kg/m3 per ASTM D1655. The slightly lower allowable density of SAF is attributed to less aromatic content in SAF produced from some pathways (Holladay et al. 2020). In 2025, U.S. jet fuel consumption was about 27 billion gallons, of which 282 million gallons (about 1%) were derived from SAF (EIA 2025d; EPA 2025a). These data reflect the enormous opportunity for SAF to capture market share and reduce the carbon intensity of the U.S. aviation sector. The focus of this section is on SAF production technologies, emerging pathways, and forecasting. The technical readiness of SAF for production is dependent upon the technology pathways; while some are mature and commercialized, others require further development and demonstration prior to market entry. SAF, as a drop-in fuel, is compatible with existing distribution and refueling infrastructure throughout the supply chain from the point of production to the delivery into aircraft.
